title: Margot Finch's Zestful Surprise
markdown:
Margot Finch could whip up something from dust bunnies, but mostly it just became more dust bunnies. She was an experimenter, a tinkerer of potions that were always a surprise. Her workshop smelled faintly of burnt eyebrows and, sometimes, mysteriously, of cheese. Her big dream was to impress Sir Aubrey, a knight whose armor gleamed brighter than a disco ball and whose coin purse jingled with an eagerness that often outpaced his good sense. Sir Aubrey loved a spectacle. Margot, bless her ink-stained fingers, was a master of the spectacular sham.

Her latest grand illusion was the Elixir of Eternal Zest. What did it do? Honestly, Margot was a bit fuzzy. It was supposed to inject pure oomph into your life. Maybe make your socks finally cooperate and stay paired, or give you the vim to do a cartwheel on demand. She brewed it in her dingy lab, where the spiders were probably better alchemists, humming a tune that sounded like a grocery list. “Needs more sparkle.” “Did the hamster escape again?”

Whoosh. In strode Sir Aubrey, armor blinding, mustache twitching. He eyed the chaotic lab. With a flourish that sent glitter poofing into the air, Margot announced, “Sir Aubrey, my esteemed patron. Prepare yourself. The Elixir of Eternal Zest. Boundless energy, a radiant complexion, and the astonishing ability to fold a fitted sheet on the first try.”

Sir Aubrey’s eyes widened. Fold a fitted sheet. Perfectly. This was huge. “My good woman,” he boomed, his voice like a trombone, “I am utterly captivated. This is the future.” With a flourish of his very large coin purse he handed over a hefty sum. Suddenly the dismal workshop became Finch’s Fantabulous Formulas, all shimmering silks and bubbling beakers that looked scientific, even if the formulas were mostly colored water and fizzy powder.

The Elixir of Eternal Zest did work. Just not as advertised. Mrs. Higgins could now yodel the entire history of her petunias. Young Timmy developed an uncontrollable urge to tap-dance on his dining room table, much to his mashed potatoes’ dismay. Old Mr. Fitzwilliam, the quietest man in town, began speaking exclusively in bizarre rhyming limericks. It was a riot of silliness. The townsfolk, roaring with laughter at first, began to grumble. Sir Aubrey’s shine faded. His knights yodeled during drills. His butler served tea while reciting odes to teacups.

“Margot, my dear,” he huffed one afternoon, helmet askew, “this zest is causing a considerable kerfuffle. My reputation is teetering more than a juggling clown on a unicycle. And my investments are energetic.” Margot’s heart did a frantic little jig of panic. Then a plump audacious pigeon waddled in. With one decisive gulp it devoured the last, suspiciously vibrant berry that was supposedly the Elixir’s secret ingredient. Poof. The last whisper of magic vanished.

“Margot Finch, you have failed me spectacularly,” Sir Aubrey roared, his face the alarming color of a bruised aubergine. “You have bamboozled me. I shall expose your utter lack of talent. Every last farthing you squandered will be accounted for.” He stormed out, the clang of his armor echoing. Margot was alone among silent beakers.

Dejected, she began packing. Her fingers brushed a dusty tome on a high shelf. Ancient Herbal Wisdom. She had always dismissed such things as dreadfully dull. As she flipped the yellowed pages she saw diagrams of common weeds and wildflowers. Notes on their soothing properties. Nothing as dramatic as yodeling. Undeniably helpful.

A new idea, small and quiet but sturdy, began to bloom. She gathered lavender, chamomile, and peppermint from her overgrown garden. She brewed them carefully, respectfully. Then, with a sprinkle of her old showmanship, a theatrical flourish and a confident smile, she presented her new creations at the town market. Finch’s Fabulous Flora. Tranquil Tisane. Grumble-Belly Brew. The townsfolk, tired of accidental yodeling, approached with cautious curiosity. They tried them. They actually, wonderfully, gloriously worked. No more impromptu limericks. A gentle soothing sense of well-being.

Sir Aubrey, armor still gleaming but spirit less so, heard whispers. Grumbling, he made his way back to Margot’s stall. He saw people smiling, truly happy, not just comically bewildered. He saw a new kind of profit, built on genuine relief.

“Margot,” he admitted, a hint of his old twinkle returning, “perhaps there is more to this Fabulous Flora than I first imagined. It appears wholesome.”

Margot Finch sold another bottle of Grumble-Belly Brew, and Sir Aubrey, after a cautious sip, did not yodel even once.
characters: Margot Finch (failed alchemist), Sir Aubrey (investor knight)
